stem: Which operation is an example of primary tillage?

options.content: Ploughing with a mouldboard plough
options.rationale: Correct: the first, deep working of the soil.

options.content: Harrowing to break clods
options.rationale: Harrowing is secondary tillage.

options.content: Raking a garden bed to a fine tilth
options.rationale: Raking is secondary tillage.

options.content: Forming ridges for sweet potatoes
options.rationale: Ridging is secondary tillage.

explanation: Primary tillage (ploughing, digging) breaks and turns the soil; secondary tillage refines it.

stem: What is the main purpose of stumping when new land is cleared?

options.content: To remove stumps and roots that damage implements
options.rationale: Correct: stumps also send up new shoots.

options.content: To add organic matter to the topsoil before planting
options.rationale: Removing stumps does not add organic matter.

options.content: To make the soil more acid for crops
options.rationale: Stumping has no such aim.

options.content: To provide shade for the young crop
options.rationale: Stumps give no shade.

explanation: Stumps and roots damage ploughs and send up new shoots, so they are dug or pulled out.

stem: Why should land not be ploughed when the soil is very wet?

options.content: Wet soil cannot be turned by any plough
options.rationale: It can be turned, but the result is poor.

options.content: The soil smears and forms hard clods and compacted layers
options.rationale: Correct: wet soil loses its structure.

options.content: Ploughing wet soil kills every earthworm in the field at once
options.rationale: This is not the main reason.

options.content: Water in the soil rusts the plough at once
options.rationale: Rust is not the reason.

explanation: Plough when the soil is moist but crumbly to keep a good structure.

stem: Which seedbed is most suitable for onion seed in a nursery?

options.content: A rough, cloddy seedbed
options.rationale: Small seeds fall into gaps and dry out.

options.content: Freshly ploughed soil that has not been harrowed
options.rationale: It is far too cloddy for small seed.

options.content: A fine, firm, level seedbed
options.rationale: Correct: small seeds need close contact with moist soil.

options.content: High ridges 30 cm tall
options.rationale: Ridges suit tubers, not small seeds in a nursery.

explanation: Small seeds are sown shallowly and need a fine tilth.
hints: How big is an onion seed?

stem: Ploughing to the same depth every year has formed a hard layer about 20 cm down. Which implement can break it without turning the soil?

options.content: A spike-tooth harrow pulled twice
options.rationale: It works only the surface.

options.content: A garden rake
options.rationale: A rake works only the top few centimetres.

options.content: A roller
options.rationale: A roller compacts rather than loosens.

options.content: A ripper (chisel plough)
options.rationale: Correct: narrow tines loosen the pan.

explanation: Rippers and subsoilers loosen compacted layers and are used in conservation farming.
hints: The implement must reach below 20 cm.

stem: Why do many farmers plough soon after harvest while the soil is still moist?

options.content: The summer crop can then be planted in winter without any water
options.rationale: Summer crops are not planted in winter.

options.content: Moist soil adds nitrogen to the plough
options.rationale: Ploughs do not gain nitrogen.

options.content: Residues are buried and rot before planting, and weeds are killed
options.rationale: Correct: it also exposes soil pests.

options.content: It removes the need for any secondary tillage
options.rationale: A seedbed is still needed before planting.

explanation: Early ploughing is easier in moist soil, buries residues to decompose and controls weeds and pests.
hints: What happens to buried residues over the dry season?

stem: A farmer on a sandy slope wants to cut soil erosion but keep yields. Which tillage system is best?

options.content: Ploughing up and down the slope every year
options.rationale: This speeds runoff and erosion.

options.content: Burning residues and ploughing twice
options.rationale: Bare, loose soil erodes badly.

options.content: Minimum tillage with a permanent mulch
options.rationale: Correct: it protects the soil and conserves moisture.

options.content: Harrowing to a very fine tilth across the whole field
options.rationale: A fine bare tilth crusts and erodes easily.

explanation: Mulch and little disturbance reduce runoff and erosion and keep moisture in the soil.
hints: Which system keeps the soil covered?

stem: What are tied ridges used for in dry areas?

options.content: To drain water quickly off the whole field after heavy storms
options.rationale: They hold water, not drain it.

options.content: To make room for tractor wheels
options.rationale: That is not their purpose.

options.content: To stop birds eating the seed
options.rationale: Ridges do not deter birds.

options.content: To hold rainwater where it falls so that it soaks in
options.rationale: Correct: the cross-ties form small basins.

explanation: Tied ridges are a water-harvesting method in low-rainfall areas.

stem: Harrowing is a secondary tillage operation that breaks clods and levels the soil.
explanation: True. It follows ploughing to prepare the seedbed.

stem: Minimum tillage usually needs less fuel and draught power than conventional ploughing.
explanation: True. Only planting lines or basins are worked, but more weed control is usually needed.

stem: Match each operation with its main purpose.

right.content: Break clods and level the surface
Firm loose soil round small seeds
Form raised rows for tuber crops
Remove stumps and roots from new land
Break and turn the soil, burying weeds

explanation: Each operation has a different job in land preparation.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: The first, deep working of the soil is called {{blank:a}} tillage; the hard layer formed by ploughing at the same depth every year is called a plough {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Primary tillage; plough pan.

stem: A worker digs about 50 m² of soil per hour with a hoe. Assume this rate. How many hours will it take to dig 0.25 ha?
explanation: 0.25 ha = 2,500 m²; 2,500 ÷ 50 = 50 hours. Forgetting to change hectares to m² gives a tiny answer.
workedSolution: 1. 0.25 ha = 2,500 m²; 2,500 ÷ 50 = 50 hours. Forgetting to change hectares to m² gives a tiny answer.

stem: An ox plough cuts a furrow 25 cm wide. Calculate the distance, in km, the oxen walk to plough 0.5 ha.
A tractor plough works a strip 1.0 m wide at 5 km/h with a field efficiency of 80%. Calculate the time, in hours, to plough 6 ha.
explanation: Theoretical rate = 1.0 × 5,000 = 5,000 m²/h = 0.5 ha/h; effective = 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4 ha/h; 6 ÷ 0.4 = 15 h. Ignoring efficiency gives 12 h, which is too short.
hints: Rate in m²/h = width × speed in m/h.
Multiply by the efficiency, then divide the area by the rate.

stem: Name the hand tool used to dig out tree stumps and roots when clearing land.
explanation: A **mattock** (or pick and axe).

stem: Explain **two** reasons for preparing land before planting maize.

points.description: Weeds are buried or uprooted.
So they do not compete with the maize for water, nutrients and light.
The soil is loosened (aerated, better infiltration).
So roots penetrate easily, and seed has good contact with moist soil for germination.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Ploughing buries weeds, so they do not compete with the young maize for water and nutrients. It also loosens the soil, so air and water enter and the roots grow easily, and the harrowed seedbed gives the seed good contact with moist soil.

explanation: Action plus effect.
hints: Give the action and its effect on the crop.

stem: Describe the steps Tatenda should follow to clear a piece of bush for cropping without causing soil erosion.

points.description: Survey the land; keep trees on steep slopes, stream banks and for windbreaks.
Slash undergrowth and fell the trees in the dry season.
Stump (dig or pull out stumps and roots) and remove stones.
Build contour ridges and waterways before ploughing, and plant a crop or cover soon after.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Tatenda should survey the land and mark trees to keep. In the dry season he slashes, fells the trees and digs out stumps and stones. Before ploughing he builds contour ridges and waterways and then plants quickly so the soil is not left bare.

explanation: Survey, clear, stump, protect.
hints: Plan, clear, stump, then protect the soil.

stem:
A research station compared two tillage systems for maize on the same sandy soil over one season.

| Treatment | Rain lost as runoff (%) | Soil lost (t/ha per season) | Maize yield (t/ha) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Conventional (plough and harrow) | 34 | 18.5 | 3.2 |
| Minimum tillage with mulch | 12 | 4.1 | 3.6 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage reduction in soil lost under minimum tillage, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in maize yield under minimum tillage, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why less soil was lost under minimum tillage.

points.description: The mulch covers the soil and absorbs the impact of raindrops, so less soil is splashed.
Less runoff (12% compared with 34%) means less water flows over the surface to carry soil away.
Undisturbed soil keeps its structure and roots, so particles are held together.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest why the maize yield was higher under minimum tillage.

points.description: More rain soaked in rather than running off, so the crop had more water in dry spells.
Less topsoil and nutrients were lost / the mulch kept the soil cooler and moister.

explanation: Interpret a tillage trial: soil loss, runoff and yield.

stem: Rudo has been allocated 2 ha of bush near Chinhoyi. There are 64 trees to remove. Two workers can each dig out about 4 stumps a day (assume this rate).

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of days the two workers will take to remove all the stumps.
parts.explanation: 4 × 2 = 8 stumps a day; 64 ÷ 8 = 8 days. Forgetting the second worker gives 16 days.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 4 × 2 = 8 stumps a day; 64 ÷ 8 = 8 days. Forgetting the second worker gives 16 days.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What should Rudo do before ploughing the cleared land for the first time?

options.content: Spread lime evenly over the whole area
options.rationale: Lime may be needed, but erosion control comes first.

options.content: Build contour ridges and waterways
options.rationale: Correct: newly cleared soil is very easily eroded.

options.content: Harrow the land to a fine tilth
options.rationale: Harrowing follows ploughing.

options.content: Plant a maize seedbed nursery
options.rationale: Maize is sown directly.

parts.explanation: Conservation works protect bare soil before the first rains.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State **three** uses Rudo could make of the trees she removes.

points.description: Poles for fencing, building or tobacco barns.
Firewood or charcoal.
Brush laid along contours as trash lines to slow runoff / mulch.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe how she should carry out primary and secondary tillage on the cleared land.

points.description: Plough (or rip) along the contour when the soil is moist, to a depth of about 15-25 cm.
Harrow to break clods and level the soil, removing remaining roots and stones.
Prepare the seedbed to suit the crop (medium tilth for maize), across the slope.

parts.explanation: Primary then secondary, along the contour.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **three** reasons why Rudo might choose conservation agriculture rather than conventional ploughing after the first season.

points.description: Less erosion because a mulch covers the soil.
More moisture conserved for dry spells.
Less labour and draught power needed / organic matter builds up over time.

explanation: Plan clearing and tillage of new land and weigh up tillage systems.
hints: Days = stumps ÷ (stumps per worker per day × workers).
Think about the soil after clearing.

stem: Farai is preparing land for three crops: finger millet, groundnuts and sweet potatoes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the seedbed needed for finger millet and give a reason.

points.description: Fine, firm, level seedbed.
The tiny seed is sown shallowly and needs close contact with moist soil.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe the seedbed for groundnuts and give a reason.

points.description: Medium tilth in loose, well-drained soil.
Large seeds germinate well with a few small clods, and pegs need loose soil to enter.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why sweet potatoes are planted on ridges.

points.description: Ridges give a deep, loose soil in which the storage roots can swell.
They drain well and make lifting easier at harvest.

explanation: Match the seedbed to the crop.
hints: Match the tilth to the seed or planting material.
